core.title: Input-validation tests assert on rejection
core.given: A test marked as an input-validation test by its task term
core.then: It MUST drive the malformed/missing/adversarial input named by the acceptance through the production boundary and assert its rejection for that specific invalid condition, witnessed by any of the stack's recognized rejection signals — an error or throw expectation, a client-error response (e.g. 400/422), or an invalidity/rejection expectation.
prefer: Construct the malformed, missing, boundary or adversarial value the acceptance names.
Send it through the same boundary production receives.
Assert the acceptance-specific rejection through the stack's rejection-assertion idiom: the exact error, a client-error response (e.g. 400/422), a rejection or invalidity expectation, or a throw.
When accepting the bad input could create or mutate state, also assert that the rejected request left that protected side effect absent.
avoid: Testing only a well-formed payload (it proves only that the parser works on good input; a well-formed payload proves nothing about adversarial input).
Triggering some unrelated error and treating any rejection as proof (a signal-based check may not flag this, but it does not witness the declared invalid condition).
Bypassing the production validation boundary with a direct fixture assertion.
core.why: An input-validation acceptance is about bad input, which a happy-path test never touches — the same silent-green-gap shape as security-auth. It is grouped with the security family because unvalidated input is the entry point for most of what the security rules defend against.
evidence: The test contains a rejection assertion tied to the declared invalid condition.
The case would turn red if validation for the declared bad input were removed.
The observed failure is caused by the intended validation rule, not by test setup.
Where invalid input could mutate state, the test asserts no protected side effect occurred.
verification: Scope: only tests whose task term marks them as input-validation tests are scanned — any such test, existing or new; there is no phase or changed-file restriction, and tests without the task term are out of scope. The carrier of the task term is profile data (for this realization, the test URN's kind segment, per urn.test).

Check: a static scan of the test body for rejection signals taken from the stack's rejection-assertion idiom (idiom.rejection_assertion); it fires only when no listed signal is present, and any one of the listed signals satisfies the check.

The check does not cover: whether a present rejection signal targets the declared invalid condition (an unrelated error passes the signal check), whether the bad input was driven through the production boundary, or the conditional protected-side-effect assertion.

values: input-validation test without a rejection assertion

fires: An input-validation test submits only a well-formed payload and asserts success.
An input-validation test asserts only on the shape of returned data and contains no rejection assertion.
doesNotFire: A test that carries none of the input-validation task terms.
An input-validation test that asserts the specific error thrown for the declared malformed input, or the client-error response (e.g. 422) returned for it.

profileRequirements.meaning: The shape of a test URN and where its kind segment — the carrier of the task term — sits; the core selects input-validation tests by task term and the realization reads the term from this carrier.
profileRequirements.bunValue: test URN carrying dash-delimited kind segments; bun.json states the segment form only — `-INPUT-`, `-VALIDATION-`, `-VALIDATE-` — not the full URN shape

profileRequirements.meaning: The concrete constructs of the stack's test runner that count as asserting rejection of invalid input; the rule's check accepts any one of the listed signals.
profileRequirements.bunValue: .rejects, toThrow, 400, 422, invalid, reject, or an error expectation

proposedKeys.meaning: URN shape of a test artifact, in particular where its kind segment — the carrier of the test's task term — sits.
proposedKeys.bunValue: test URN carrying dash-delimited kind segments (`-INPUT-`, `-VALIDATION-`, `-VALIDATE-`); bun.json states the segment form only, not the full URN shape
proposedKeys.whyNoExistingKey: The urn group's artifact params (component, acceptance, smoke_acceptance, train, wmbt, wagon, feature, journey) include no test artifact, so no existing urn.<artifact> or urn.binding.<artifact> key can express a test URN's shape or its kind segment.

proposedKeys.meaning: The concrete constructs of the stack's test runner that count as asserting rejection of invalid input; a check for a rejection assertion accepts any one of the listed signals.
proposedKeys.bunValue: .rejects, toThrow, 400, 422, invalid, reject, or an error expectation
proposedKeys.whyNoExistingKey: idiom.error_types describes how production code types and raises errors, not how a test asserts rejection; no other idiom key covers test-assertion syntax.

bunOnly.text: 'A Bun test' — the runtime's own test format
bunOnly.reason: The runtime name has no stack-neutral equivalent; the INPUT/VALIDATION/VALIDATE terms stay with the rule and their carrier (the test URN's kind segment) is profile data (urn.test).

bunOnly.text: e.g. `expect(() => parseOrder({ sku: null })).toThrow("INVALID_SKU");` or, over HTTP, `expect(res.status).toBe(422);`
bunOnly.reason: Concrete example code of the Bun test runner; bun.json itself is delivered as the reference example, so the snippet is not repeated in the core.

The vocabulary's tooling.languages documents languages of production source, not languages whose test files this rule scans, and production and test languages need not coincide; no key covers test-scan languages, so the language restriction stays with the Bun realization.

The detector/validator id of this one rule is a realization detail (notProfileKeys); the core names the check generically (a scan for absence of any rejection assertion, needing a new observer that parses test bodies).

bunOnly.text: Detector: identifies input-validation tests from the URN and flags those with no rejection assertion (implementation: validator bun_tester_discipline_detector).
bunOnly.reason: The validator id and the URN-based identification mechanics are realization details; the generic behavior (flag input-validation tests lacking any rejection assertion) is kept in core:verification and the carrier is profiled as urn.test.

neutralityNotes: What could not be kept fully neutral, and where each part went: (1) the exact rejection-signal list — the portable witnesses (an error or throw expectation, a client-error 400/422 response, an invalidity/rejection expectation) stay in the core's then and prefer[2], while the runner-specific assertion syntax is exposed as the proposed profile key idiom.rejection_assertion (string value holding the exact Bun signal list), with its any-one-signal rule kept in core verification; (2) the task-term carrier — the test URN's kind segment is profile data via the proposed key urn.test (the urn group has no test artifact); the INPUT/VALIDATION/VALIDATE terms stay with the rule, and bun.json states only the segment form, not the full test-URN shape or its binding syntax; (3) the language activation fact (typescript/javascript, 'Bun test runtime') — the vocabulary's tooling.languages documents languages of production source, not test-scan languages, and no key covers the latter, so the language restriction stays with the Bun realization rather than being repurposed from a production key; (4) file_kind 'test' remains a generic value that each stack maps to concrete test file kinds through the profile's suffix keys, which bun.json does not state. Severity 4 / strict disposition are rule-level and stayed in core:verification rather than becoming profile keys. The detector, validator and finding ids are bunOnly per the notProfileKeys policy.
